[Highway Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.00387) interpolate transformed and identity features: y=T(x)H(x)+(1−T(x))x. Negative gate biases encourage initial identity propagation, easing deep-network optimization; this does not establish that strong biases help select between two convolution scales. For y=(1−g)S+gL, g=σ(z), direct differentiation gives ∂y/∂z=g(1−g)(L−S). Thus saturation and similar branch outputs independently weaken gate learning. At z=−5, the sigmoid derivative is approximately 0.00665 versus 0.25 at zero. Shared convolution weights can encourage branch similarity, although differing dilations need not produce similar outputs. These are mathematical implications, not measured NextItNet results.

Gated temporal convolutions typically modulate features rather than interpolate receptive fields: [WaveNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.03499) uses tanh(A)⊙σ(B); [Dauphin et al.](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/dauphin17a.html) use A⊙σ(B), retaining a linear content path. Neither directly tests adaptive short/long-scale selection. [Selective Kernel Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.06586) provide the closer comparison: multiple receptive-field branches, pooled context, and input-dependent channelwise softmax weights. For two branches, softmax selection is equivalent to a sigmoid of their logit difference. SK’s spatial pooling would require causal adaptation for sequential training.

Useful NextItNet controls: fixed short-only, long-only, and 50:50 interpolation; learned input-independent per-layer/channel gates; then input-dependent gates with matched initial mixing. Compare zero, moderate, and strongly biased logits under the same training budget. Measure gate means, across-input variation, saturation, gradient norms, and normalized branch differences/cosine similarity. These distinguish initialization effects, redundant branches, learned global scale preference, and contextual adaptation. Keep all branches jointly trained inside one causal residual network and one checkpoint per category.
